                       1                                           INTRODUCTION
                       2          Plaintiff twists himself in knots trying to avoid the parties’ contractually agreed-upon forum
                       3   selection clause. As Mr. Cooper explained at length in its Opening Memorandum, the Northern
                       4   District of Texas is the proper venue for this case. It is required by both (1) the parties’ binding
                       5   forum selection clause, and (2) a traditional 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) analysis. Plaintiff’s attempts to
                       6   avoid transfer on both grounds are unpersuasive.
                       7          Plaintiff does not dispute that he agreed to and accepted Mr. Cooper’s Terms, and the
                       8   incorporated forum selection clause. He also does not contest that the clause is presumed valid and
                       9   should be enforced under binding Supreme Court precedent. Nor does he contest that, when
                      10   voluntarily creating a Mr. Cooper online account, he inputted his account-creation information, and
                      11   immediately below those fields was the prominently displayed text: “By clicking ‘Save and
                      12   Continue’ you agree to the Terms of Use for Mr. Cooper’s website,” with “Terms of Use” bolded,
                      13   in bright blue, and hyperlinked to Mr. Cooper’s Terms. See ECF 25-5. Proximately under that text
                      14   was the button “Save & Continue,” which Plaintiff does not deny clicking. Instead, Plaintiff
                      15   suggests that Mr. Cooper’s Terms are “unenforceable ‘sign-in wrap’” based on two false premises.
                      16   First, Plaintiff’s major premise—expressed through his counsel only and not by sworn
                      17   declaration—is that he would not have “expected to be agreeing to a whole new array of terms and
                      18   conditions with a new servicer” when his loan was transferred to Mr. Cooper. ECF 29 at 1–13. But
                      19   Plaintiff fundamentally confuses loan terms and website terms. There is no allegation that Mr.
                      20   Cooper changed the terms of Plaintiff’s loan, nor do his loan terms concern this case, which is about
                      21   Mr. Cooper’s alleged use of advertising trackers on its website. Plaintiff could pay his mortgage
                      22   through several different means; that he chose to do so by creating an online account was not forced
                      23   upon him. Thus, when he voluntarily clicked and agreed to the “Terms of Use for Mr. Cooper’s
                      24   website,” he accepted those terms and the forum selection clause. Second, Plaintiff’s minor premise
                      25   is that the “Terms of Use” hyperlink was not adequately visible when Plaintiff clicked to agree to
                      26   the Terms. While Plaintiff tries to make this argument based on his shrinkage of two full webpages
                      27   down to a half-page in his brief, his tricks of illusion cannot save him. The Ninth Circuit and this
                      28

                       1   District have repeatedly enforced webpages with similar (and even less conspicuous) disclosures
                       2   of terms and assent. Plaintiff’s attempt to distinguish those cases falls flat.
                       3          As for the Section 1404(a) analysis, Plaintiff provides no basis for his conclusion that the
                       4   case should stay in California. Although Plaintiff asserts (at 12) that he “chose to file this case in
                       5   California,” he does not dispute that a plaintiff’s choice of forum in a class action lawsuit is given
                       6   “minimal deference.” ECF 24 at 10. Likewise, Plaintiff does not even address the vast majority of
                       7   the factors that favor transfer—e.g., the interests of justice, location of relevant events, access to
                       8   proof, cost of litigation, forum’s contacts with the claims, relative court congestion, and familiarity
                       9   with the governing law. Rather, he relies upon only unsupported rhetoric. And while the Amended
                      10   Complaint eliminated two named plaintiffs in a manufactured effort to avoid the conclusion that
                      11   this case should be transferred, the Section 1404(a) factors still overwhelmingly support transfer.
                      12   At bottom, this putative class action lawsuit concerns “allegations about Mr. Cooper’s website,
                      13   policies and procedures, and actions ..., all of which occurred in Texas, the forum in which Mr.
                      14   Cooper is located has a vastly greater connection to the claims.” Id. at 8–9.
                      15          Plaintiff’s Opposition confirms that this case belongs in Texas and that the Court should
                      16   grant the transfer to the Northern District of Texas.
                      17                                               ARGUMENT
                      18   I.     The Parties’ Forum Selection Clause Requires Transfer.

                      19          A.      Plaintiff Does Not Dispute Agreeing to Mr. Cooper’s Terms.

                      20          Plaintiff does not dispute that he created an online account with Mr. Cooper, in which he

                      21   clicked “Save and Continue” above which states: “By clicking ‘Save and Continue,’ you agree to

                      22   the Terms of Use for Mr. Cooper’s website,” where the words “Terms of Use” are in bold and a

                      23   bright blue font, are against a white background, and are clearly hyperlinked to the Terms, and the

                      24   surrounding text is grey to draw the user’s attention to the “Terms of Use.” ECF 24 at 1–13. He

                      25   also does not dispute that the forum provision was conspicuous within the Terms, and squarely

                      26   covers this case. See id. He tellingly submits no testimony or facts at all to contest the record

                      27   presentation by Mr. Cooper. As to the law, he does not dispute that forum selection clauses are

                      28   presumed valid and are enforced, and that this case is not an “exceptional case[]” that would permit

                       2   Ct. for W. Dist. of Tex., 571 U.S. 49, 56–57 (2013); M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co., 407 U.S.
                       3   1, 10, 15 (1972)).
                       4          Rather, Plaintiff maintains only that (1) ”[w]hen a mortgage is transferred to a new
                       5   mortgagee, the consumer does not expect her rate to change or the terms of a long-term financial
                       6   product to shift,” and (2) a consumer would not understand that he is agreeing the Terms of Use by
                       7   clicking “Save and Continue.” ECF 29 at 1–12. The Court should reject these erroneous claims. 1
                       8          B.      Plaintiff’s Loan Transfer Does Not Alter His Express Assent to the Terms.
                       9          Plaintiff’s effort to avoid his agreement to the forum selection provision because his
                      10   mortgage loan was previously serviced by a prior lender is too clever by half. Plaintiff’s confusion
                      11   on this point is all the more mystifying in light of his central allegations in the Amended Complaint
                      12   that he agreed to Mr. Cooper’s online Privacy Policies and Terms— which he specifically alleges
                      13   form “Privacy Contracts” and representations that underpin all of his claims. See, e.g., ECF 26 ¶¶
                      14   28, 78, 79, nn. 7, 29. Plaintiff cannot on the one hand allege that the online Privacy Policy was an
                      15   agreement with him that created obligations independent of his mortgage, while on the other assert
                      16   that the online Terms did not and that it would be confusing for any consumer to understand that
                      17   an online account agreement is separate and apart from a previously entered mortgage contract.
                      18   Plaintiff cannot pick and choose which contractual provisions he wishes to understand, wishes to
                      19   understand, and when.
                      20          Further, Plaintiff misapprehends his own case: the Amended Complaint 2 alleges that Mr.
                      21   Cooper’s website improperly used advertising trackers, not that Mr. Cooper changed his loan terms.
                      22   E.g., ECF 26 ¶ 3 (“Mr. Cooper … knowingly and secretly configur[ed] and implement[ed] code-
                      23   based tracking devices … into its Website.”). Thus, his repeated arguments that a hypothetical

                      26   Cooper’s pending Motion to Dismiss the Amended Complaint. ECF 30.

                       2   mortgage is transferred to a new mortgagee, the consumer does not expect her rate to change or the
                       3   terms of a long-term financial product to shift.”); see also, e.g., id. at 2–3 (“Mr. Cooper is trying to
                       4   enforce ‘bonus’ terms” additional to the “terms of the mortgage agreement”), 6 (“Imagine receiving
                       5   a notice that one’s … interest rate was [] changing.”); 7 (“Beltran would not have expected to be
                       6   agreeing to a whole new array of terms and conditions with a new servicer”), 8 (a consumer “is not
                       7   expecting to be bound by ‘bonus terms’ from some random company that purchased the right to be
                       8   paid on his mortgage”). It further makes no sense because the standard federal mortgage agreement
                       9   grants the original lender the right to transfer the servicing rights, without alteration of the terms,
                      10   which is a public fact that is common, and widely understood. See, e.g., California-Single Family-
                      11   Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac Uniform Instrument, Form 3005, ¶ 22 (July 2021) (“The Loan Servicer
                      12   may change one or more times during the term of the Note. The Loan Servicer may or may not be

                      14   instruments/form-3005-california_deed-of-trust_07.2021.docx; What happens if the company that
                      15   I send my mortgage payments to changes?, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (Apr. 3, 2024),
                      16   available   at    https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-happens-if-the-company-that-i-
                      17   send-my-mortgage-payments-to-changes-en-215.
                      18          By contrast, Plaintiff does not, and cannot, challenge that a consumer would understand
                      19   that, when registering an online account for a new website—and clicking “‘Save and Continue,’
                      20   [to] agree to the Terms of Use for Mr. Cooper’s website”—he is agreeing to that website’s Terms.
                      21   ECF 29 at 5. Indeed, the Ninth Circuit and courts in this District routinely enforce nearly identical
                      22   agreements to online terms of use when registering an account. See ECF 24 at 4–5 (citing cases).
                      23   Plaintiff does not cite any authority that creating an online account on a new website after a
                      24   mortgage transfer makes the new website’s Terms any less enforceable. It does not: consumers
                      25   readily understand that they are using a new website when they affirmatively register a new account
                      26   with the new website and agree to its terms, separate and apart from a different company’s website
                      27   that previously serviced the mortgage. Plaintiff himself admits he had no confusion that he was

                       2   Coooper bought out the mortgage and so Plaintiff Beltran opened an online account with Mr.
                       3   Cooper.”); id. ¶ 124 (Bank of America “directed him to Mr. Cooper,” where he “set up an account
                       4   with Mr. Cooper”); id. ¶ 128 (“Beltran opened an online account with Mr. Cooper”). And he does
                       5   not dispute that, to do so, he clicked to agree to the hyperlinked “Terms of Use for Mr. Cooper’s
                       6   website.” Likewise, Plaintiff’s claim that the Terms are an “adhesion contract” because “[i]nternet
                       7   contracts … are mostly contracts of adhesion [since] consumers do not generally have the ability
                       8   to negotiate” ECF 29 at 2, 4, runs contrary to established law. 3 Indeed, courts in the Ninth Circuit
                       9   routinely enforce online Terms, and do not find them inherently adhesive. See ECF 24 at 4–5 (citing
                      10   cases enforcing online Terms). Plaintiff simply ignores this wall of authority. The Terms, then,
                      11   should be enforced.
                      12          Plaintiff’s arguments about the “context” of the Terms, ECF 29 at 5–8, rest on his attempt
                      13   to conflate website terms with loan terms, and they are wrong. For example, Plaintiff suggests,
                      14   without support, that the website Terms supply “bonus” terms to the underlying “mortgage
                      15   agreement.” ECF 29 at 2, 7–8, 11. Again, this argument rests on the fiction that consumers cannot
                      16   differentiate between a mortgage originator and later servicer, as most consumers accept in a
                      17   standard mortgage agreement. Regardless, website terms govern the use of a website irrespective
                      18   of an underlying contract, and they do so here. Mr. Cooper’s website Terms—including the forum
                      19   provision—govern the use of the website, not substantive terms of the loan. See ECF 24-2 at 7
                      20   (“The user’s access to and use of the Mr. Cooper websites and mobile apps, and the terms of this
                      21   disclaimer are governed by all applicable Federal laws and the laws of the state of Texas; and the
                      22   user agrees that venue shall be located in Dallas County, Texas.”); see, e.g., Johnson v. Walmart
                      23   Inc., 57 F.4th 677, 682 (9th Cir. 2023) (online terms of use governed “access to and use of all
                      24   Walmart Sites” whereas Walmart Auto Center’s tire servicing agreement covered the disputed in-
                      25   store engagement). Plaintiff’s ancillary references to loan-related actions—e.g., foreclosure actions
                      26

                       3   Terms. 4
                       4          It is unsurprising, then, that Plaintiff can cite nothing to support that website terms supply
                       5   “bonus terms” to mortgage agreements, or are “adhesive” because his loan was transferred. ECF
                       6   29 at 3–8. Again, they are not. Plaintiff admits that he affirmatively took steps to open a new
                       7   account on a new website (which was not a condition to continue to access or pay his mortgage),
                       8   and clicked “Save and Continue” to agree to the new website Terms. Rhetoric aside, there is nothing
                       9   “surreptitious” or “imposi[ing]” about that. Id. at 7; see Amculture Trading, Inc. v. Renaissance
                      10   Imports, Inc., 2011 WL 13217697, at *1 (C.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2011) (rejecting plaintiff’s arguments
                      11   in opposition to defendant’s motion to transfer as “merely conclusory” and lacking “any discussion
                      12   of [supporting] facts”).
                      13          The cases Plaintiff cites to suggest that the nature of his transaction with Mr. Cooper did
                      14   not create an expectation of an ongoing relationship shows just how wide of the mark he is here. In
                      15   Chabolla v. ClassPass Inc., 129 F.4th 1147 (9th Cir. 2025), there was ambiguity as to whether the
                      16   context of the transaction indicated “‘some sort of continuing relationship ... that would require
                      17   some terms and conditions,’” due to indications that “[t]he transaction … [is] a one-time purchase”
                      18   and the fact that “[t]he user does not create a username or password and is not asked to make an
                      19   account.” Id. at 1155 (citation omitted). Just the opposite here: Plaintiff admits that he entered a
                      20   username and password to create an online account. ECF 26 ¶¶ 123–24; ECF 29 at 8–12. And there
                      21   is no doubt that he anticipated an ongoing relationship when, to “pay his [monthly] mortgage, [he]
                      22   … set up an account with Mr. Cooper.” ECF 26 ¶¶ 123–24; see also id. ¶ 126 (“Beltran regularly
                      23   uses Mr. Cooper’s website”); id. (“He has been using the website anywhere between a few times a
                      24   month to a few times a week since 2021-2022”). Courts in this District find that users had

1           On October 8, 2025, this Court entered an order sua sponte referring this case to the
2
     Honorable Jacqueline Scott Corley for consideration of whether this case is related to Case No.
3
     3:25-cv-04412-JSC, Beltran v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC. Defendant Lakeview Loan Serving,
4
     LLC (“Lakeview” or “Defendant”) responded on October 12, 2025. D.E. 37. 1 Plaintiffs hereby
5

6    respond that the cases do not meet the definition of a “related case” pursuant to the Local Rule and

7    should not be related or consolidated on their respective dockets.
8
            In the proposed case management order, Lakeview explicitly represented that it was
9
     unaware of any case meeting the definition of a “related case” as defined by Local Rule 3-12. D.E.
10
     30 at 6, ¶ 10. In full, Lakeview said:
11

12          Related Cases. The parties are unaware of any cases that meet the definition of a
            “related case” as defined in Civil Local Rule 3-12. Lakeview notes, however, that
13          plaintiffs’ counsel have sued one of Lakeview’s subservicers (Mr. Cooper) in
            Beltran v. Nationstar Mortgage LLC, No. 4:25-cv-04412-JSC (N.D. Cal.), asserting
14
            similar claims and facts, and it notes relevant overlap in facts and claims may
15          become evident at some point in these cases.

16   Id. There being no disagreement between the parties that there is no case meeting the “related case”
17
     definition, Plaintiffs did not see reason to further comment regarding Lakeview’s vague
18
     anticipation that there “may” be overlap of claims and facts “at some point.” D.E. 30 at 6, ¶ 10.
19
     Plaintiffs could hardly directly respond to such hypotheticals; further, each party is the master of
20

21   its own discrete assertions in the case management order.

22

23
            1
24             The deadline for this Notice Response is today, October 14, 2025. See D.E. 35 (order
     issued under LR 3-12(c), which incorporates LR 3-12(e) for responses in opposition or notices of
25   support, and in turn follows the timing of LR 7-11 which provides a “4 day” response after the
     triggering event). Because the Court’s initial order was entered October 8, 2025, the four-day
26
     deadline, which excludes Sundays and federal holidays, is October 14. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1)(B,
27   C); Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(6)(A). Notably, counsel for Plaintiffs emailed Defendant’s counsel on
     October 13, 2025, requesting that the parties stipulate to a response deadline for Plaintiffs of
28   Friday, October 17 (an extension of three days from the deadline). Lakeview declined to stipulate
     to the extension.
                                          2
     PLAINTIFFS’ RESPONSE TO CASE RELATION NOTICE- Case No.: 3:25-cv-04412-JSC
              Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC           Document 32        Filed 10/14/25       Page 3 of 6



1           As Lakeview now avers in a footnote, D.E. 37 at 2, n.1, it has had a late-breaking epiphany
2
     that apparently, yes, the cases are indeed related. Id. (“In light of Judge Thompson’s referral to this
3
     Court to consider relatedness, Lakeview has conducted additional factual research and confirmed
4
     the cases are indeed related as explained below.”). Additional factual research indeed.
5

6           Local Rule 3-12(a) is quite clear about what constitutes a “related case.” The actions must

7    “concern substantially the same parties, property, transaction, or event” and there will be
8
     duplication of labor amongst the Court’s Judges. It does not say that the cases should be “similar,”
9
     “comparable,” or “concern the same bad conduct.” It says: “substantially the same.”
10
            Completely absent from Lakeview’s response is any indication that the defendants in these
11

12   cases are formally related as corporate entities. Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC (represented here

13   by Quinn Emanuel) is not the same party as Nationstar Mortgage, LLC d/b/a Mr. Cooper
14
     (represented in Case No. 3:25-cv-04412-JSC by Goodwin Proctor). Lakeview’s filing reveals that
15
     Nationstar Mortgage, LLC d/b/a Mr. Cooper, sometimes does business with Lakeview. D.E. 37 at
16
     2 (noting Mr. Cooper is a subservicer of Lakeview). Lakeview then expends several pages (and
17

18   offers several declarations) indicating that some loans of one entity may be serviced by another

19   entity. Just because two companies in the same industry are sued for the same kind of conduct does
20
     not mean the cases are related. The companies may do business together, but that is not a basis to
21
     find that they are the same party—as Lakeview admits, they are not.
22
            Notably, Lakeview concedes “Lakeview and Mr. Cooper are independent entities[.]” D.E.
23

24   37 at 3. At bottom, Lakeview has merely contended that it is a frequent business partner with Mr.

25   Cooper and that each company may have contractual relationships with the other implicating the
26
     servicing of the plaintiffs’ mortgages in these two cases. Any possibility (if any) that the
27
     companies’ websites may be partially entangled does not itself raise a question of relatedness under
28


                                           3
      PLAINTIFFS’ RESPONSE TO CASE RELATION NOTICE- Case No.: 3:25-cv-04412-JSC
              Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC           Document 32        Filed 10/14/25      Page 4 of 6



1    the Rules. These entities explicitly chose to structure their mortgage servicing (and data harvesting)
2
     businesses this way. But LR 3-12(a) is unconcerned about their side deals. Surely, doing some
3
     business together some of the time does not equate to the two discrete entities comprising
4
     “substantially the same parties.”
5

6           While certainly these cases concern similar conduct, that does not render them the same

7    “transaction or event.” Cases can be similar but not sufficiently related to satisfy the Local Rule.
8
     See, e.g., ASUS Computer Int’l v. Interdigital, Inc., No. 15-CV-01716-BLF, 2015 WL 13783764,
9
     at *1 (N.D. Cal. June 15, 2015) (“There are, undoubtedly, some similarities between the suits:
10
     Interdigital is a party to both suits, both ASUS and Pegatron have licensing agreements with
11

12   Interdigital that were allegedly violated, and Interdigital alleges that these licensing agreements

13   include an enforceable arbitration provision.”) (finding cases were not related); Hodges v. Akeena
14
     Solar, Inc., No. CV 09-02147 JW, 2010 WL 2756536, at *1 (N.D. Cal. July 9, 2010) (“Here, the
15
     Court finds that although the two actions concern substantially the same transaction and events,
16
     the legal claims, named defendants, and procedural posture are different.”).
17

18          The companies operate different websites. D.E. 31, ¶ 30 (this case); Case No. 3:25-cv-

19   04412-JSC, D.E. 26 at ¶ 29. Lakeview has had Meta Pixel installed on its systems since October
20
     of 2021, D.E. 26 at ¶ 43, whereas Mr. Cooper employed tracking systems on its website between
21
     May 2019 and at least May 2025. Case No. 3:25-cv-04412-JSC, D.E. 26 at ¶ 54. The disclosures
22
     each defendant made to tech companies through these technologies may differ. These are some,
23

24   but not all possible relevant distinctions. Lakeview avers in its filing that: “Or, worse yet, both

25   defendants could potentially be held liable for the same alleged data privacy violations if the
26
     factfinders each find the defendant in their case responsible for the same webpage if plaintiffs seek
27
     to blur the line between where Lakeview’s website ends and Mr. Cooper’s website begins.” D.E.
28


                                          4
     PLAINTIFFS’ RESPONSE TO CASE RELATION NOTICE- Case No.: 3:25-cv-04412-JSC
              Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC           Document 32         Filed 10/14/25       Page 5 of 6



1    37 at 5 (emphasis in original). Lakeview’s attempt to cast aspersions on the plaintiffs in these cases
2
     is undermined by its own conflicting representations. Discovery can bear out these distinctions—
3
     it is not the fault of the plaintiffs in either case (ordinary consumers) that these companies set their
4
     websites up this way or have agreements between each other. Nor is it a sufficient basis under LR
5

6    3-12(a) to find that they are “substantially the same.” The only blurring of the lines being done

7    here is by Lakeview. Mr. Cooper is liable for what happens on its website, and Lakeview is liable
8
     for what happens on its website.
9
             These cases may concern similar conduct, but they do not concern “the same” parties,
10
     transactions, or events. They should proceed separately. Consistent with Local Rule 3-11(e), this
11

12   response is being filed on both dockets.

13

                       1                        MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

                       2          This case joins a constellation of cases arising from the nearly ubiquitous use of advertising

                       3   trackers on websites. Unlike most web tracking cases, though, Plaintiff concedes that he consented

                       4   to the data practices at the heart of his kitchen-sink Complaint. While Plaintiff’s core theory is that

                       5   Mr. Cooper discloses certain website interactions to third parties for advertising “without

                       6   authorization,” he admits he entered into “Privacy Contracts,” in which he agreed that Mr. Cooper

                       7   may do just that: “Third parties may [] use [tracking] technologies” for “[t]arget[ed] [a]dvertising,”

                       8   ECF 26-1, and Mr. Cooper may “share personal information, such as commercial info, internet

                       9   activity, and inferences, with advertising and social media services to deliver personalized

                      10   advertisements.” RJN, Ex. 3. While Plaintiff could have opted out of the alleged data sharing, he

                      11   did not. Because the Complaint is premised entirely on the disclosures having been “unauthorized,”

                      12   it crumbles with Plaintiff’s consent. The Complaint fails for other reasons as a matter of law.

                      13          First, Plaintiff lacks standing to pursue any claims. Standing requires that Plaintiff establish

                      14   a concrete injury, that is traceable to Mr. Cooper. Plaintiff does not. Plaintiff consented to the

                      15   alleged disclosures and so suffered no injury; and he does not plausibly allege that any of his private

                      16   and financial information was actually disclosed, let alone that he was harmed by any supposed

                      17   disclosure. Plaintiff’s amendments only confirm this fundamental flaw. Plaintiff added that he:

                      18   (i) “interact[ed]” with several public webpages, but does not allege that he input any information,

                      19   let alone any private information, ECF 26 ¶¶ 125–26; and (ii) input information to create an online

                      20   account in 2021, but does not allege that any such information was collected or disclosed, id. ¶¶
                      21   124, 137. Plaintiff, therefore, does not allege any disclosure of his personal information, much less

                      22   any “‘highly offensive’ interferences or disclosures” that could confer standing. Popa v. Microsoft

                      23   Corp., – F.4th –, 2025 WL 2448824, at *5 (9th Cir. Aug. 26, 2025). In fact, Plaintiff admits that he

                      24   received ads about the mortgages and real estate listings at a time when he admittedly was shopping

                      25   online for a mortgage, which strains credulity as an injury. And he does not allege any such ads

                      26   were traceable to Mr. Cooper as opposed to any other mortgage company or more plausible source.
                      27          Second, Plaintiff’s claims for monetary relief are barred by the limitation-of-liability

                      28   provision that he agreed to when creating an online account. That provision precludes recovery for

                       2   Plaintiff’s claims arise in connection with the website, so he is barred from pursuing damages.

                       3          Third, for similar reasons, Plaintiff’s common-law and statutory claims fail. His claims rest

                       4   on generic allegations that non-personal data was shared with third parties for advertising, which

                       5   might: breach unidentified contracts; be negligent or intentional; or violate statutes. Plaintiff’s

                       6   consent, again, forecloses a breach of any duty, and his claims separately fail as a matter of law.

                       7          Finally, most of Plaintiff’s claims are time-barred to the extent they are premised on

                       8   information he allegedly provided when creating an account in 2021—nearly four years before his

                       9   initial complaint. Because that is the only information Plaintiff alleges to have provided through

                      10   Mr. Cooper’s website, his claims independently must be dismissed.

                      11          The Complaint should be dismissed in its entirety, with prejudice.

                      18   make payments.” Id. ¶¶ 124–26. Specifically, the amended Complaint now alleges:

                                     webpages, titled “calculators,” “refinance,” “buy a home,” “rates,” “apply,” “help,” “get
                      20             cash from equity,” “sign in,” and “buying or selling a home.” Id. ¶¶ 125–26. Plaintiff does
                                     not contend to have input any information on those webpages, private or otherwise. Id.

                      26   or on any particular webpage (including on the account-registration page in 2021). See id. ¶ 126.

                      11            A court must dismiss a complaint under Rule 12(b)(1) if a plaintiff does not satisfy Article
                      12   III standing. Brown v. Christiana Tr., 722 F. App’x 702, 702 (9th Cir. 2018). Plaintiff bears the
                      13   burden of establishing standing. Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330, 330 (2016), as revised (May
                      14   24, 2016). To establish standing, Plaintiff “must have (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly
                      15   traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a

                      22   a personal and individual way,” and “concrete[]” if it is “‘de facto’; that is, it must actually exist.”

                      10                                           LEGAL STANDARD

                      11           On a motion to dismiss, courts may consider “matters of judicial notice.” United States v.

                      12   Ritchie, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003). In particular, courts may judicially notice “a fact that is

                      13   not subject to reasonable dispute because it: (1) is generally known within the trial court’s territorial

                      14   jurisdiction; or (2) can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot

                      15   reasonably be questioned.” Fed. R. Evid. 201(b). Courts are required to grant a valid request for

                      16   judicial notice. Fed. R. Evid. 201(c) (“The court … must take judicial notice if a party requests it

                      17   and the court is supplied with the necessary information” (emphasis added)). Documents that

                      18   “appear on publicly available websites” are “proper subjects for judicial notice.” Brown v. Google

                      19   LLC, 525 F. Supp. 3d 1049, 1061 (N.D. Cal. 2021) (granting request for judicial notice in support

                      20   of motion to dismiss); see also Daniels-Hall v. Nat’l Educ. Ass’n, 629 F.3d 992, 998–99 (9th Cir.
                      21   2010) (noticing publicly available websites).

                      22           Also, in deciding a motion to dismiss, a court “must consider … documents incorporated

                      23   into the complaint by reference.” Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rts., Ltd., 551 U.S. 308, 322

                      24   (2007). The doctrine of incorporation by reference “treats certain documents as though they are

                      25   part of the complaint itself.” Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir.

                      26   2018). When a claim depends on the contents of a document attached to the motion to dismiss, and
                      27   the document’s authenticity is unquestioned, the court may deem the document “incorporated” into

                       5   upon which their claims are based,’ a court may consider a writing referenced in a complaint but

                      11   Plaintiff tries to selectively quote and paraphrase the Terms and Privacy Policy, contending they

                      12   comprise “Mr. Cooper’s [p]rivacy [r]epresentations,” and he pleads the Privacy Policies as

                      15   representations in the Terms and Privacy Policies and “without their knowledge or authorization.”

                      16   Id. ¶¶ 3, 6–7, 38, 45, 53; see Swartz, 476 F.3d at 763, supra. And the Terms are additionally central

                      18   pleads claims under California law and seek monetary damages, ECF 26 ¶¶ 179–224, 251–304,

                      20   limitation-of-liability provision that precludes recovery for monetary relief. See Ex. 1 (“use of the

                      22   limitations provision). Therefore, the Court should incorporate by reference the Terms and State-

            Plaintiff Martin Beltran, individually and on behalf of all others similarly situated

7
     as follows.
8
                                             INTRODUCTION
9
            1.      Plaintiff brings this class action to address Defendant’s outrageous, illegal, and
10

11
     widespread practice of disclosing—without consent—the Nonpublic Personal Information1 and

12   Personally Identifiable Financial Information2 (together, “Personal and Financial Information”) of

13   Plaintiff and the proposed Class Members to third parties, including Meta Platforms, Inc. d/b/a
14
     Meta (“Facebook” or “Meta”), Google, LLC (“Google”), Microsoft Corp. (“Microsoft”),
15
     DoubleClick, NewRelic, Optimizely, HotJar, and possibly others (collectively the “Third Parties”)
16

17
     (in short, “the Disclosure”).

18          2.      Mr. Cooper is a massive mortgage lender and servicer that provides services to

19   customers across the globe and the United States, including in California. To provide these
20
     services, Mr. Cooper operates and encourages its customers to use its website,
21

22
            1
                The United States Congress defines “nonpublic personal information” as “personally
23
     identifiable financial information-- (i) provided by a consumer to a financial institution; (ii)
24   resulting from any transaction with the consumer or any service performed for the consumer; or
     (iii) otherwise obtained by the financial institution.” The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, 15 U.S.C.A.
25   § 6809(4)(A) (“GLBA”).
              2
                “Personally identifiable financial information means any information: (i) A consumer
26
     provides to [a financial institution] to obtain a financial product or service from [the financial
27   institution]; (ii) About a consumer resulting from any transaction involving a financial product or
     service between [a financial institution] and a consumer; or (iii) [a financial institution] otherwise
28   obtain[s] about a consumer in connection with providing a financial product or service to that
     consumer.” 16 C.F.R. § 313.3(o)(1).
                                                 2
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC            Document 26        Filed 09/08/25     Page 3 of 86



1
     https://www.mrcooper.com/ (the “Website”), on which customers can, among other things, access
2
     their account information, manage their mortgage, obtain information about Mr. Cooper’s services,
3
     calculate and obtain quotes for mortgage payments and refinancing options, and apply mortgages
4

5    or refinancing.

6           3.         Despite its unique position as a massive and trusted mortgage lender and servicer,
7
     Mr. Cooper used its Website to blatantly collect and disclose Consumers’3 and Customers’4
8
     (collectively, “Customers”) Personal and Financial Information to Third Parties uninvolved in the
9
     provision of mortgage services—entirely without their knowledge or authorization. Mr. Cooper
10

11   did so by knowingly and secretly configuring and implementing code-based tracking devices

12   (“trackers” or “tracking technologies”) into its Website.
13
            4.         Through these trackers, Mr. Cooper disclosed and continues to disclose Personal
14
     and Financial Information that Customers input into and accessed on Mr. Cooper’s Website. This
15
     information includes without limitation, the user’s status as a customer; whether the customer is
16

17   logged in to Mr. Cooper’s website; the user’s browsing activities, including that the user clicked

18   certain buttons and what URLs or webpages they led to; the user’s refinancing options and
19
     customer selection; the reason the customer is seeking to refinance; that the user submitted a
20
     mortgage and/or refinancing application; the user’s request for a quote and a summary of the user’s
21
     selections; the type of property at issue; the state where the user’s property is located; and the
22

23

24
            3
                The term “consumer” means “an individual who obtains or has obtained a financial
25   product or service . . . that is to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, or
     that individual’s legal representative.” 16 C.F.R. § 313.3; 15 U.S.C.A. § 6809(9).
26            4
                “Customer means a consumer who has a customer relationship with [a financial
27   institution].” 16 C.F.R. § 313.3. “The term ‘time of establishing a customer relationship’ shall . . .
     in the case of a financial institution engaged in extending credit directly to consumers to finance
28   purchases of goods or services, mean the time of establishing the credit relationship with the
     consumer.” 15 U.S.C.A. § 6809.
                                                   3
                                        CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC            Document 26        Filed 09/08/25      Page 4 of 86



1
     user’s current stage of the homebuying process.
2
            5.      Upon information and belief, Mr. Cooper utilized data from trackers to improve
3
     and to save costs on its marketing campaigns, improve its data analytics, attract new customers,
4

5    and generate sales. Mr. Cooper benefited from use of Customers’ Personal and Financial

6    Information. Mr. Cooper further allowed the Third Parties, who are uninvolved in Mr. Cooper’s
7
     provision of mortgage services, to profit from its Disclosure of Customers’ Private and Financial
8
     information. And the Third Parties used Customers’ Personal and Financial Information for
9
     themselves and disclosed to fourth parties who also profited off of it. Facebook, for example, will
10

11   use the data collected from Customers of Mr. Cooper to sell ads to fourth parties who will further

12   profit off the use of that information
13
            6.      Customers like Plaintiff and Class Members simply do not anticipate that a trusted
14
     mortgage lender and servicer will send their Personal and Financial Information to hidden Third
15
     Parties (who in turn share with fourth parties), all of whom profit off of it. Likewise, when Plaintiff
16

17   and Class Members used Defendant’s Website, they thought they were communicating exclusively

18   with a trusted mortgage lender and servicer for the sole purpose of obtaining mortgage information
19
     and/or services.

            7.      At no time did Mr. Cooper disclose to Plaintiff or Class Members that it was sharing
21
     their Personal and Financial Information with the Third Parties for third- and fourth-party use.

23   Plaintiff and Class Members never signed a written authorization permitting Defendant to send

24   their Personal and Financial Information to the Third Parties who were uninvolved in the provision
25
     of financial services.
26
            8.      Defendant owed a variety of duties, including common law, statutory, contractual,
27
     and regulatory duties, to keep Plaintiff’sand Class Members’ Personal and Financial Information
28

                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC            Document 26        Filed 09/08/25       Page 5 of 86



1
     safe, secure, and confidential.
2
             9.      Furthermore, by obtaining, collecting, using, and deriving a benefit from
3
     Plaintiff’sand Class Members’ Personal and Financial Information, Defendant assumed legal and
4

5    equitable duties to those individuals to protect and safeguard their information from unauthorized

6    disclosure.

             10.     The statutory and regulatory duties Mr. Cooper owed Customers include its
8
     obligations under federal law. For example, the GLBA requires that “each financial institution has
9
     an affirmative and continuing obligation to respect the privacy of its customers and to protect the

11   security and confidentiality of those customers’ nonpublic personal information.” 15 U.S.C. §

     disclosing a Customer’s Personal and Financial Information without sufficient advance

16

17   requirements, by disclosing Customers’ Personal and Financial Information without proper

18   advance notification and opt-out rights as required under the GLBA.

     indistinguishable from the types of information Mr. Cooper disclosed to Facebook, Google, and

     Microsoft, including, among other things: (a) “[i]nformation a consumer provides to [Mr. Cooper]

25
     product or service from [Mr. Cooper]”; (c) “information about [Mr. Cooper] consumer . . .
26
     disclosed in a manner that indicates that the individual is or has been [Mr. Cooper] consumer”; and
27
     (d) “any information [Mr. Cooper] collect[s] through an Internet ‘cookie’ (an information
28


                                                  5
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC           Document 26       Filed 09/08/25      Page 6 of 86



1
     collecting device from a web server).” 16 C.F.R. 313.3(o)(2)(i).
2
            13.     Mr. Cooper breached its duties under California state law, including, for example,
3
     the California Consumer Privacy Act. That statue provides California consumers with rights to
4

5    control their personal information including the right to know what personal information is being

6    collected about them and whether that information is sold or disclosed and to whom, the right to
7
     prohibit the sale of their personal information, and the right to request deletion of their personal
8
     information. Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100, et seq. Mr. Cooper breached its obligations under this
9
     statute by, for example, failing to provide Customers with appropriate notice that their information
10

11   was being disclosed to Third Parties for third- and fourth- party use. The notice and consent Mr.

12   Cooper purports to provide and obtain, through the policies it provides on its website, is not
13
     appropriate or sufficient, as a reasonable Consumer would not have understood those policies as
14
     notifying them of Mr. Cooper’s disclosure of their Personal and Financial Information to Third
15
     Parties for third- and fourth- party use.
16

17          14.     Mr. Cooper breached its common law, statutory, and contractual obligations to

18   Plaintiff and Class Members by, inter alia, (i) failing to adequately review its marketing programs
19
     and web based technology to ensure its Website was safe and secure; (ii) failing to remove or
20
     disengage technology that was known and designed to collect and share Personal and Financial
21
     Information; (iii) aiding, agreeing, and conspiring with the Third Parties to intercept
22

23   communications sent and received by Plaintiff and Class Members; (iv) failing to obtain the written

24   consent of Plaintiff and Class Members to disclose their Personal and Financial Information to
25
     Third Parties for Third Party and fourth party use; (v) failing to protect Personal and Financial
26
     Information and take steps to block the transmission of Plaintiff’sand Class Members’ Personal
27
     and Financial Information through the use of tracking technology; (vi) failing to warn Plaintiff and
28


                                                  6
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-04412-JSC          Document 26         Filed 09/08/25     Page 7 of 86



1
     Class Members; and (vii) otherwise failing to design and monitor its Website to maintain the
2
     confidentiality and integrity of its customers’ Personal and Financial Information.
3
            15.     Plaintiff seeks to remedy these harms and brings causes of action of Negligence;
4

5    Violation of the Comprehensive Computer Data Access And Fraud Act (“CDAFA”), Cal. Penal

6    Code § 502; Violation Of California’s Consumer Protection Law (“UCL”), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code
7
     §§ 17200, et seq.; Violation of California Consumer Privacy Act (“CCPA”), 1798.100, et seq.;
8
     Breach of Express and Implied Contract; Unjust Enrichment; Breach Of Confidence; Violation of
9
     The California Invasion of Privacy Act (“CIPA”), Cal. Penal Code §§ 631, et seq.; Violation of
10

11   Invasion of Privacy Act, Cal. Pen. Code §§ 632, et seq.; Violation of Invasion of Privacy Act, Cal.

12   Pen. Code §§ 638.51, et seq.; and Violation of The Electronic Communications Privacy Act
13
     (“ECPA”), 18 U.S.C. §§ 2511(1), et seq.

            16.     Plaintiff brings this action, individually and on behalf of all others similarly

     situated, for damages and equitable relief.
